One of the teachers of the law came and heard them debating. Noticing that Jesus had given them a good answer, he asked him, “Of all the commandments, which is the most important?” “The most important one,” answered Jesus, “is this: ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one.  Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no commandment greater than these.”

First Peter 4:8 says, “Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins.” We are not intended to love so that something happens, but simply to love with all our heart, mind, soul, and strength.

Your “heart” is your passions and desires. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Loving God with your heart also means loving Him with and through your emotions. We don’t love only within fair weather but also in the tempest.

Your soul is what Jesus purchased on the cross. Our soul is of the highest value, and nothing can be measured against it. Matthew 16:26 says, “What good will it be for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul? Or what can anyone give in exchange for their soul?” Your soul is the eternal part of you that will go on forever. Another way to think about your soul is as your will. The good news is that God gave us free will so when we love with our soul, we are choosing to love or deciding to love with our whole being.

Loving God with your strength is letting Him have your time, your sweat, your abilities, and your possessions. When we surrender our strengths, we no longer must count on ourselves. Our strength is finite but His is infinite. Philippians 4:13 says, “I can do all this through him who gives me strength.” God’s infinite strength is available to us when we need it. “That is why, for Christ’s sake, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

Knowledge: Facts and information acquired through experience using all our senses. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; but fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Proverbs 1:7).

Skills: Specific things we develop through repetition in learned activities. “Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank” (Proverbs 22:29).

Ability: Performance of natural, innate skills strengthened through practice over time. “Each of you should use whatever gift you have received to serve others, as faithful stewards of God’s grace in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10).

Excellence grows through faithful repetition.  “Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord” (Colossians 3:23). Choose one deliberate, learnable practice, and start showing up to it consistently. Record your plan.

Where are you competent, and where is God inviting you toward expertise? “But solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained themselves to distinguish good from evil” Hebrews 5:14. Name the shortcuts you’ve been tempted to take.

Stay curious; stay teachable. “He has filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills” (Exodus 35:31). Plan your next learning stretch: a book list, a course, shadowing a seasoned practitioner, or teaching what you know to someone newer. Ask where your craft can bless others and strengthen the Body.

Psalm 46:10 says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” It is important that we learn to stop striving at times and learn to simply rest in our identity in Christ, recognizing His sovereignty and presence. The phrase “be still” in Hebrew can be defined as letting go, releasing, or stopping. In this context, it can be considered a declarative command to STOP. Psalm 46 speaks of turbulent times with war and earthquakes. This command asks us to trust that He is God and to let go of our anxieties and fears. The second part of the verse, “know that I am God,” invites us to lean not on our own understanding and accept His authority and care for all things in our lives.

At the heart of it all lies the truth of Ephesians 2:10: “For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.” This verse holds the perfect balance between being and doing. We are His handiwork—that’s our being, our identity rooted in Christ, formed by His love and redeemed by His grace. And we are created to do good works—that’s our doing, the natural outflow of who we are in Him.

Being anchors doing, but it also fuels discovery. When you rest in Christ, your actions begin to flow from love, not striving. This is where creativity, wisdom, and purpose take shape. “Remain in me, as I also remain in you. No branch can bear fruit by itself; it must remain in the vine” (John 15:4).
